question: Is there a single number that captures both how much a researcher publishes and how often that work is cited?
title: An index to quantify an individual's scientific research output
answer: The h-index: a scientist has index h if h of their papers have at least h citations each and the rest have no more than h each.

question: Why might most claimed discoveries that rest on a p below 0.05 turn out to be wrong?
title: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False
answer: The chance a finding is true (positive predictive value) depends on the prior odds of the relationship, the study's power and the significance level, so with low odds and power most claimed findings are false.

question: What do downloads from a pirate site for papers reveal about which articles people cannot get legally?
title: Looking into Pandora's Box: The Content of Sci-Hub and its Usage
answer: Of about 28 million downloads, users favour recent articles (35% published after 2013), suggesting embargoes are circumvented; chemistry is over-represented, and 80% of downloads come from just 9 publishers.

question: How fast did journals with dubious refereeing practices grow their output in the early 2010s?
title: 'Predatory' open access: a longitudinal study of article volumes and market characteristics
answer: From 53,000 articles in 2010 to an estimated 420,000 in 2014, in about 8,000 active journals, at an average charge of 178 USD per article.

question: Do softer disciplines report confirming their hypotheses more often than physics and space science do?
title: "Positive" Results Increase Down the Hierarchy of the Sciences
answer: Yes: of 2,434 papers, the odds of a positive result were about 5 times higher in psychology, psychiatry, economics and business than in space science, and 2.3 times higher in the social than the physical sciences.

question: How many academic documents in English can be found online, and what fraction can be read without paying?
title: The Number of Scholarly Documents on the Public Web
answer: At least 114 million, of which Google Scholar holds nearly 100 million; at least 27 million (24%) are freely available, from 12% to 50% depending on the field.

question: How concentrated is the output of scientific journals among a handful of companies?
title: The Oligopoly of Academic Publishers in the Digital Era
answer: The top five publishers account for more than half of all papers in 2013; 70% in the social sciences, against 20% in the humanities.

question: How often do the p-values printed in psychology articles fail to match the test statistics they come from?
title: The (mis)reporting of statistical results in psychology journals
answer: Around 18% of statistical results are incorrectly reported, and about 15% of articles hold at least one conclusion that flips significance on recalculation.

question: Do the two big commercial citation databases favour some fields and languages over others?
title: The journal coverage of Web of Science and Scopus: a comparative analysis
answer: Yes: both favour natural sciences, engineering and biomedical research over social sciences and humanities, and over-represent English-language journals, though their coverage differs.

question: When a drug company tried to repeat landmark cancer lab studies, how many held up?
title: Raise standards for preclinical cancer research
answer: Only 6 of 53 landmark preclinical studies (11%) were confirmed by Amgen's scientists.

question: How closely do two referees agree when they judge the same manuscript?
title: A Reliability-Generalization Study of Journal Peer Reviews
answer: Poorly: across 70 coefficients from 48 studies, the mean intra-class correlation was .34 and the mean Cohen's kappa .17.

question: On average, how many links must be followed to get from one random page on the internet to another?
title: Diameter of the World-Wide Web
answer: About 19: the average shortest path grows as 0.35 + 2.06 log N, giving 18.59 for 800 million documents, a small-world network.

question: How quickly did the number of articles in free-to-read journals grow during the 2000s?
title: The Development of Open Access Journal Publishing from 1993 to 2009
answer: By about 30% a year for articles and 18% for journals since 2000, reaching an estimated 191,000 articles in 4,769 journals in 2009, 7.7% of all peer-reviewed articles.

question: Do political scientists who post their articles on their own websites get cited more?
title: Will Open Access Get Me Cited? An Analysis of the Efficacy of Open Access Publishing in Political Science
answer: Yes: across eight top-ranked journals, self-archived articles show a clear citation advantage over those available only to paying readers.

question: Are psychologists who refuse to hand over their raw data more likely to have weak or mistaken results?
title: Willingness to Share Research Data Is Related to the Strength of the Evidence and the Quality of Reporting of Statistical Results
answer: Yes: across 1,148 significant results in 49 papers, reluctance to share went with weaker evidence and more reporting errors, especially errors that affect significance.

question: Can flies of the same supposedly standard wild-type stock behave differently depending on which lab they came from?
title: Sub-strains of Drosophila Canton-S differ markedly in their locomotor behavior
answer: Yes: five Canton-S sub-strains fell into three groups by walking behaviour, stripe fixation varying most, likely from founder effects.

question: Has automatically reading cancer journals been used to suggest how a lipid signal makes brain tumour cells more invasive?
title: Text mining of full-text journal articles combined with gene expression analysis reveals a relationship between sphingosine-1-phosphate and invasiveness of a glioblastoma cell line
answer: Yes: mining 20 cancer journals over five years for 72 genes pointed to S1P triggering MMP-9 through NRG-1, VEGF and uPA.

question: What share of references do authors take from other papers' bibliographies instead of from the original?
title: Stochastic modeling of citation slips
answer: About 70 to 90%, judged from repeated misprints in citations to twelve well-known papers, whose frequencies follow Zipf's law.

question: Is the free scholarly search engine a fair substitute for the commercial citation index when judging management research?
title: Google Scholar as a new source for citation analysis
answer: Largely yes: Google Scholar covers more, especially books, conference papers and non-US journals, and its h-index, g-index and citations per paper correlate strongly with the impact factor.

question: Can how openly a journal describes its refereeing predict whether it would accept a bogus paper?
title: Peer Review Quality and Transparency of the Peer-Review Process in Open Access and Subscription Journals
answer: Yes: journals rated more transparent on a 14-item tool were less likely to accept Bohannon's hoax paper and had higher h5 impact.
